summary: Overall quality is high across 9 units (ENT 2, ophthalmology 2, orthopaedics 2, urology 3). Every numeric key was recomputed (air-bone gap, PTA, shock index, ESR (age+10)/2, logMAR, OPP, target IOP, delta P, translation %, BMI, leg length discrepancy, PSAD, 5-ARI correction, MAP, urine output, Ch to mm, mean output) and all are correct. Every MCQ and true/false key was worked independently and is correct with exactly one defensible option. The stated classifications and thresholds (Gustilo-Anderson, delta P 30 mmHg, PCNL above 2 cm, torsion exploration without delay for imaging, Weber/Rinne, GCA ESR convention matching the stem) are accurate. No tab/control characters, literal \uXXXX text, placeholder steps, [object Object] or garbled characters were found. Only minor issues were found, mainly a UK diabetic-eye-screening referral pathway that needs a source check and a post-catheterisation drainage example that conflates retained residual volume with diuresis. Garden, Salter-Harris, Weber ankle, Schatzker, scoliosis, tympanometry, epiglottitis, foreign body and tonsillectomy criteria are not covered in this course and so were not assessed. This is an AI review only; the course still needs a subject-matter expert (UK clinician) before clinical reliance.

issues.problem: Worked example 'grading a screening photograph' gives the answer 'Pre-proliferative diabetic retinopathy with no maculopathy; refer to the hospital eye service' and the plan says 'refer for ophthalmic assessment (not annual routine screening)'. In the English screening programme (R grades) pre-proliferative R2 is normally managed by shorter-interval digital surveillance, with hospital eye service referral for R3 (proliferative) or maculopathy per grade. The lesson table also equates 'pre-proliferative' with 'severe non-proliferative', which are not identical across the R-grade and international scales. Unverified against the current NDESP pathway.
issues.suggestedFix: Check against the current NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme grading and outcome tables, then state the R2 outcome as short-interval (about 6-monthly) surveillance or referral per local pathway, reserving urgent HES referral for R3/M1 findings, and note that the UK R2 and international severe NPDR categories are approximately, not exactly, equivalent.

issues.problem: The explanation treats the mean of 1,800 mL over the first 6 hours as 'persistently high output after relief ... suggests post-obstructive diuresis'. In chronic retention the first drained volume is largely the retained residual urine, not new urine production, so this figure cannot show diuresis. The lesson worked example makes the same conflation by treating the first 1,500 mL in 2 h (750 mL/h) as 'urine output after relief'.
issues.suggestedFix: Distinguish the initial residual volume drained on catheterisation from subsequent hourly output. Define post-obstructive diuresis on hourly output after the residual has drained (commonly above about 200 mL/h on consecutive hours, or above about 3 L/day), and reword the q007 stem or explanation and the worked example accordingly.

issues.problem: The acute versus chronic retention table has no caption, and the residual-volume row says acute retention is 'often several hundred mL, tends to be smaller than in chronic' without defining a threshold (the callout gives only 'about 300 mL or more' for chronic). Learners cannot tell how to apply the volume criterion.
issues.suggestedFix: Add a caption and state the working definitions consistently (for example chronic retention as a persistently large residual, commonly above about 300 mL on repeated measurement, with acute retention defined by sudden painful inability to void), noting that cut-offs vary.
